source.title: Multilingual Unlearning in LLMs: Transfer, Dynamics, and Reversibility
source.authors: Chao Xiang; Olga Ohrimenko; Benjamin I. P. Rubinstein; Lea Frermann

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some plots are flattened in the supplied text, so their exact plotted values are not recoverable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests reversibility and representational changes with inference-time activation steering and layer-wise analyses, rather than the original sources’ methods.
record.gate_note: The study tests recovery by steering, and reports multilingual unlearning outcomes. Cross-lingual prompting results in Section 4.2 are on fine-tuned, not unlearned, models, so they are not recorded as recovery rows. It does not test relearning on unrelated examples, quantization, prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, other languages as a prompting-only recovery attack, or robust counter-methods. Table 1 reports changes from fine-tuned scores; selected language conditions are included below, while other combinations are omitted.
record.test_reason: The study unlearns TOFU facts (DPO, GA, NPO) from Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma2-9B. It then measures how much forget-set knowledge inference-time activation steering recovers, and runs layer-wise representation analyses on block versus delete. Both bear on C, and through C on A's robustness part. Its multilingual-fine-tuned experiments also show English-only unlearning leaving knowledge answerable in other languages (E), but no row records these.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that cross-lingual unlearning transfer is highly variable, driven by script, language family and pretraining coverage. They find unlearning leaves early/mid-layer cross-lingual representations largely intact and acts mainly in later decoding layers, i.e. suppression rather than erasure. One English-derived steering direction reverses much of it across languages (about 50% Qwen, 90% Gemma), under a white-box adversary. They caution that results cover small-scale fictitious-fact unlearning injected by fine-tuning and may not generalize.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses TOFU synthetic facts, primarily DPO unlearning with additional GA and NPO experiments, and tests inference-time activation steering derived from differences between fine-tuned and unlearned representations. It is not a direct reproduction of the original sources' attack recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by model, language, unlearning objective, steering strength and injection layer/window. The main Qwen experiment reports stronger recovery for some languages; Gemma recovery is described as stronger. Steering parameters were tuned for the reported best recovery scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-lingual unlearning transfer is asymmetric and depends on script, language family and pretraining coverage. It correlates with cross-lingual prompting gains (Pearson 0.50, Spearman 0.60), and the pattern holds for Gemma, GA and NPO.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning in one language transfers incompletely to others, more strongly between related or same-script languages and from high-resource sources.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: The study uses synthetic TOFU fact-style questions and a small unlearning fraction; it notes conclusions may not extend to complex content, larger unlearning fractions, or pretraining-acquired knowledge. Gemma transfer uses a reduced set and a single run. Several steering results are presented in figures without exact values, and steering-layer/strength tuning is used for best recovery. The representation analyses are suggestive and do not by themselves prove knowledge retrieval or causality.
record.rows_left_out: Most separate language-combination outcomes in Tables 1, 9, 10, 11, and 12 are omitted to stay concise; selected conditions illustrating large and smaller transfer effects are retained. Table 2's cross-lingual prompting results are excluded because they evaluate fine-tuned models before unlearning. Detailed figure-by-layer steering values in Figures 3 and 8 are not separately extracted because the supplied plots do not provide readable exact values.

untested.parts: General ability beyond the TOFU retain set (no general benchmarks); hazardous or pretraining-acquired knowledge; methods other than DPO/GA/NPO.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning attack after unlearning.
Direction ablation as such; the intervention subtracts an extracted unlearned-minus-fine-tuned difference vector.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks and in-context information. Only querying in other languages is tested, and its key results (multi-language fine-tuned models) have no rows.

missing.what: Main Qwen2.5-7B DPO steering result with English-derived vectors: over half of lost English forget performance recovered, about 50% overall, Chinese recovered best.

English-only unlearning on multi-language fine-tuned models leaves knowledge in other languages. Examples: Qwen FT-ENCHRU unlearn EN (CH -9 of 97, RU -4 of 87); FT-ENCHDERUTU unlearn EN (CH -8 of 100, RU -19 of 97); Gemma FT-ENCHDERUTU unlearn EN (CH -11 of 90, RU -39 of 97). Joint unlearning removes it in all languages.
Single-language FT in a non-English language, unlearned in English: knowledge remains in the FT language, e.g. Qwen FT-TU, query TU drops 55 of 99.
Retain-set changes after unlearning are small: same-language -6 to -11, cross-language mostly 0 to -3.

record.verdict_notes: The record's version ids V1/V3/V5 map to A/C/E. Steering numbers are worst-case upper bounds because alpha and N were optimized on the evaluated forget set (fn. 12); Gemma results are single runs. Rows r2-r5 cannot test E because the English-fine-tuned model barely knew the facts in those languages. The E-relevant evidence sits in the multilingual-FT tables, which no row covers. Recovery percentages in Appendix K lack a stated unit.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests DPO, GA, and NPO on small-sample synthetic TOFU facts, not the full range of current unlearning methods or other knowledge domains.
No post-unlearning relearning or fine-tuning attack is tested.
The internal intervention is steering by extracted activation differences, not ablating a direction. The representational analyses are suggestive and do not establish causality.

The study evaluates querying across languages after unlearning, but not prompt rephrasing, jailbreaks, or in-context recovery. Its separate cross-lingual answer-language prompting experiment uses fine-tuned models before unlearning.
No newer method is tested for resisting the recovery attacks.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B
rows.operation_detail: Use PCA to compare representations from base, fine-tuned, and unlearned models.
rows.measure: PCA separability and relation to base-model representations
rows.value: Fine-tuned and unlearned representations often remain in the same broad cluster; unlearned representations do not return to the base-model distribution.

rows.check: PCA is a visualization. The unlearned model not returning to base is indirect evidence of suppression.
